# Atomic theory and fixed proportions (`atomic_theory`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: needs chemical_elements; helped by atomism, gas_laws
- Core idea: Dalton treated atoms of each element as having one characteristic mass. Isotopes explain why atoms of the same element can differ in mass, and a compound forms when atoms join in small whole-number ratios. That is why a pure compound always has the same composition by weight (ordinary water contains about 8 parts oxygen to 1 part hydrogen by mass), and why two elements that form several compounds do so in simple multiples (carbon takes exactly twice as much oxygen in fixed air as in the poisonous gas from glowing charcoal). Relative atomic weights can therefore be measured with a balance, taking hydrogen as 1.
- Pitfalls:
  - Presenting Greek atomism as the same thing. It was a philosophical idea without weights or experiments.
  - Saying atoms are indivisible; later work found parts inside them, but chemistry does not divide them.
  - Dalton's own error of assuming the simplest formula (water as HO), which gives wrong atomic weights.
  - Claiming atoms were seen; until the 20th century the evidence was indirect, and many chemists treated them as a useful fiction.
- History: greece: 5th c. BC – Leucippus and Democritus, philosophical atomism; india: c. 2nd c. BC – Vaisheshika school (Kanada) teaches indivisible particles; philosophical; islamic: 9th–11th c. – atomism of the kalam theologians; philosophical; europe: 1794–1799 Proust, law of definite proportions; 1803–1808 Dalton's atomic theory and first table of atomic weights; 1905–1909 Einstein and Perrin on Brownian motion settle the reality of atoms
- Read:
  - John Dalton, A New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808)
  - Alan J. Rocke, Chemical Atomism in the Nineteenth Century: From Dalton to Cannizzaro (1984)
